domain: Project Management Fundamentals and Core Concepts
title: Project vs Program vs Portfolio
summary: Projects, programs, and portfolios represent different levels of organizational work management, from individual initiatives to strategic alignment.
key_concepts: Project = temporary, unique deliverable
Program = group of related projects managed together
Portfolio = collection of projects/programs aligned with strategy
Operations = ongoing, repetitive work

project.definition: A temporary endeavor undertaken to create a unique product, service, or result
characteristics: Has a defined start and end
project.example: Build a warehouse system for a client

program.definition: A group of related projects managed in a coordinated way

portfolio.definition: A collection of projects/programs managed to achieve strategic goals

exam_tips: Project = tactical execution. Program = benefits. Portfolio = strategy alignment. Always distinguish clearly in exam questions.

domain: Project Management Fundamentals and Core Concepts
title: Project Objective
summary: Project objectives define what the project aims to achieve in measurable and specific terms.
key_concepts: Objectives must be SMART
Linked to business value
Defined early (charter phase)
Guide scope and success criteria
exam_tips: If objective is unclear → project risk increases. PMP prefers clear, measurable objectives linked to business value.

domain: Project Management Fundamentals and Core Concepts
title: Strategic Dependencies (Project – Program – Portfolio)
summary: Dependencies at project, program, and portfolio levels define how initiatives rely on each other to deliver value, benefits, and strategic alignment.
key_concepts: Projects can depend on other projects
Programs manage interdependencies between projects
Portfolios manage dependencies to optimize strategic value
Dependencies impact sequencing, risk, and resource allocation

project_level_dependency.definition: A project may rely on outputs, resources, or timing of another project
examples: Project B depends on Project A delivering a system first
Infrastructure project must complete before application rollout

program_level_dependency.definition: Program coordinates multiple related projects with strong interdependencies
examples: ERP implementation program: finance module depends on core system
Digital transformation with multiple integrated systems
impact: Delays in one project affect the entire program

portfolio_level_dependency.definition: Portfolio manages dependencies across projects/programs to align with strategy
examples: Investment prioritization based on dependency and ROI
Delay of one program impacts strategic roadmap

dependency_types.description: One initiative requires output of another
A capability must exist before another initiative starts
Alignment or sequencing driven by business strategy

exam_tips: Projects have dependencies. Programs MANAGE dependencies. Portfolios OPTIMIZE dependencies aligned with strategy.

domain: Project Management Fundamentals and Core Concepts
title: PMI Code of Ethics and Professional Conduct
summary: The PMI Code of Ethics defines the expected behavior of project management professionals through four core values: Responsibility, Respect, Fairness, and Honesty.
key_concepts: 4 Core Values: Responsibility, Respect, Fairness, Honesty
Applies to all PMI members and practitioners
Guides ethical decision-making
Important for exam situational questions

core_values.name: Responsibility
core_values.definition: Take ownership of decisions and actions
pm_application: Escalate issues instead of hiding them

core_values.name: Respect
core_values.definition: Show consideration for people and culture

core_values.name: Honesty
pm_application: Do not hide delays or issues

ethical_scenarios.scenario: Project delay but PM hides it
Selecting vendor based on personal relationship

exam_tips: If a scenario involves unethical behavior, ALWAYS choose transparency, accountability, and professional integrity. PMI strongly favors honesty and escalation over hiding issues.

domain: Project Management Fundamentals and Core Concepts
title: Constraints, Assumptions, and Risks
summary: Constraints, assumptions, and risks are key elements that influence project planning, execution, and uncertainty management.
key_concepts: Constraints limit project execution
Assumptions are treated as true without proof
Risks represent uncertainty (positive or negative)
All three impact planning and decision-making

constraints.definition: Limiting factors that affect the execution of a project

assumptions.definition: Factors considered to be true without proof for planning purposes
risks_associated: If assumption is wrong → becomes a risk

risks.definition: An uncertain event or condition that can have a positive or negative effect on project objectives

exam_tips: Assumptions create risk. Constraints limit options. Risks must be actively managed throughout the project lifecycle.

domain: Project Management Fundamentals and Core Concepts
title: Product, Product Life Cycle, and Project Life Cycle
summary: Products and projects operate on different lifecycles. Projects create products, while products evolve over a longer product life cycle.
key_concepts: Project creates product
Project life cycle is temporary
Product life cycle is long-term
Multiple projects can exist within one product life cycle

product.definition: A product is a tangible or intangible output that delivers value to customers or users.

product_lifecycle.definition: The full life span of a product from idea to retirement.
characteristics: Focused on value delivery and market performance
examples: A SaaS product evolving over years
Retail product from launch to phase-out

project_lifecycle.definition: The series of phases that a project passes through from initiation to closure.
examples: Build version 1 of a mobile app

relationships: Multiple projects can exist within one product life cycle
Product life cycle continues after project ends
Programs may manage multiple projects contributing to a product
exam_tips: Project life cycle is temporary. Product life cycle is long-term. A project delivers a product, but the product continues after the project ends.

domain: Project Management Fundamentals and Core Concepts
title: Working with OPAs and EEFs
summary: EEFs are environmental conditions that constrain or influence the project and cannot be controlled, while OPAs are internal organizational assets that can be used to support project work.
key_concepts: EEFs must be accepted and adapted to
OPAs can be used, reused, and sometimes updated
EEFs can be internal or external
OPAs are always internal

EEFs.definition: Conditions outside the direct control of the project manager that influence or constrain project execution.
characteristics: Can positively or negatively impact project

OPAs.definition: Organizational assets such as processes, templates, and knowledge repositories that support project execution.

exam_tips: EEFs = conditions you cannot control. OPAs = assets you can use. Policies are OPAs even if you must follow them.

domain: Project Management Fundamentals and Core Concepts
title: Project Development Approach
summary: A project development approach defines how project work is organized, planned, and executed to deliver outcomes. The main approaches include Predictive, Agile (Adaptive), and Hybrid.
key_concepts: Development approach determines how work is done
Three main types: Predictive, Agile, Hybrid
Choice depends on uncertainty, requirements stability, and environment
Approach influences planning, execution, and control

predictive.definition: A development approach where scope, schedule, and cost are defined early and changes are controlled.

agile.definition: An adaptive approach that delivers value through iterative and incremental work cycles, allowing continuous feedback and improvement.

iterative.definition: A development technique where the product is repeatedly refined and improved through multiple cycles.
characteristics: Feedback used to enhance product quality

incremental.definition: A development technique where the product is built and delivered in small, usable portions.
incremental.focus: Delivering new value step by step

agile.example: A product is developed through multiple iterations where the team continuously improves existing features while also delivering new features in increments.

hybrid.definition: A combination of predictive and agile approaches used together in a project.

exam_tips: Predictive = stable requirements. Agile = changing requirements. Hybrid = mix both depending on project context.

domain: Project Management Fundamentals and Core Concepts
title: Tailoring in Project Management
summary: Tailoring is the process of adapting project management approach, processes, and practices to fit the specific needs of a project.
key_concepts: No one-size-fits-all approach
Tailoring adapts methods to project context
Driven by project complexity, risk, and environment
Applies to both predictive and agile approaches

details.definition: The deliberate adjustment of project management processes, tools, and techniques to match the project's context and needs.
why tailoring: Projects differ in size, complexity, and risk

exam_tips: PMI always supports tailoring. The best approach is the one that fits the project, not strictly following all processes.

domain: Project Management Fundamentals and Core Concepts
title: Uncertainty and Complexity
summary: Uncertainty and complexity influence how projects are managed, requiring adaptive thinking, risk awareness, and appropriate development approaches.
key_concepts: Uncertainty relates to unknowns
Complexity comes from interactions and dependencies
Higher uncertainty drives agile approaches
Requires continuous assessment and adaptation

uncertainty.definition: A lack of clarity or predictability regarding project outcomes, requirements, or environment.

complexity.definition: The degree of interrelated parts, interactions, and dependencies that make a project difficult to manage.
impact: Need for strong communication and governance

exam_tips: High uncertainty = Agile. Low uncertainty = Predictive. Complexity increases the need for collaboration and adaptability.

domain: Project Management Fundamentals and Core Concepts
title: Project Governance
summary: Project governance is the framework of policies, processes, and structures that guide project decisions, ensure alignment, and provide oversight.
key concepts: Defines roles, responsibilities, and decision rights
Applies across project, program, and portfolio levels

details.definition: A structured framework that defines how projects are directed, controlled, and monitored.

exam_tips: Governance ensures control and alignment. It defines who makes decisions and how the project is monitored.

title: Predictive Approach — Overview
summary: The predictive (Waterfall) approach is a plan-driven methodology where project scope, schedule, and cost are defined upfront before execution begins. Work is performed in a sequential and structured manner.
key concepts: Plan-driven approach with detailed upfront planning
Formal change control for all modifications

details.definition: An approach where scope, time, and cost are determined early in the project lifecycle, and changes are managed through formal control processes.
details.real world example: Construction of a building where all specifications, budget, and timeline must be defined before execution. Any change requires formal approval.

exam_tips: Predictive is ideal for stable requirements and low uncertainty. Common in construction, manufacturing, and regulated industries.

title: Process Groups Overview
summary: Process Groups are logical groupings of project management activities that guide a project from initiation to closure. They are interconnected, overlapping, and iterative rather than strictly sequential.
key concepts: They overlap and iterate throughout the project
Outputs from one group feed into others

Initiating.purpose: Define and authorize the project or phase

Planning.purpose: Define the roadmap to achieve project objectives

Executing.purpose: Perform the work defined in the plan

details.interaction model: Executing and Monitoring & Controlling operate in parallel while Planning may be revisited as changes occur.

exam_tips: Process Groups are overlapping and iterative. Monitoring & Controlling occurs throughout the entire project lifecycle.

title: Knowledge Areas Overview
summary: Knowledge Areas represent specialized domains of project management expertise. Each area focuses on a specific aspect of managing a project.
key_concepts: Knowledge Areas group related processes
Each process belongs to both a Process Group and a Knowledge Area
Together they form the foundation of predictive project management
Integration Management connects all knowledge areas

knowledge_areas.name: Integration Management
knowledge_areas.purpose: Ensure all project components are properly coordinated

knowledge_areas.name: Scope Management
knowledge_areas.purpose: Define and control what is included in the project

knowledge_areas.name: Resource Management
knowledge_areas.purpose: Manage project team and physical resources

knowledge_areas.name: Governance & Control (Extended View)
knowledge_areas.purpose: Provide oversight, decision-making, and alignment with strategy

details.relationship: All knowledge areas are integrated through Integration Management and interact continuously throughout the project lifecycle.

exam_tips: Every process belongs to both a Process Group and a Knowledge Area. Integration Management is central and connects all others.

title: Process Groups × Knowledge Areas Matrix (49 Processes)
summary: This matrix maps all project management processes across Process Groups and Knowledge Areas, forming the foundation of predictive project management.
key_insights: Each process belongs to one Process Group and one Knowledge Area
Planning contains the largest number of processes
exam_tips: Understand where each process belongs. Integration processes appear across all groups and are central to project control.

title: Integration Management (Deep Dive)
summary: Integration Management ensures all project elements work together. It is the central coordination function in project management.
key_concepts: Project Manager owns integration
All knowledge areas are connected through integration
Trade-offs are managed here
Change control is centralized
examples: Balancing schedule delay vs cost increase
Deciding whether to approve a scope change
exam_tips: If the question involves coordination, trade-offs, or change control → Integration Management is the answer.

title: Project Management Plan
summary: The Project Management Plan (PMP) is the comprehensive document that describes how the project will be executed, monitored, controlled, and closed.
key concepts: Integrated document combining all subsidiary plans
Contains scope, schedule, and cost baselines
A living document updated through change control
Central reference for managing the project

details.definition: A formal document that integrates and consolidates all subsidiary plans and baselines to guide project execution and control.
baselines: Scope Baseline (Scope Statement + WBS + WBS Dictionary)
important distinctions: Charter defines WHAT and WHY; PMP defines HOW
PMP is detailed, while the Charter is high-level
Baselines are approved versions of plans
details.real world example: Like an operations manual that outlines processes, schedules, responsibilities, and controls required to run a complex system.

exam tips: The Project Management Plan defines how the project will be executed. It is approved before execution and updated only through change control.

title: Project Charter
summary: The Project Charter formally authorizes the project and grants the Project Manager authority to use organizational resources.
key_concepts: Formal authorization of the project
Grants authority to the Project Manager
Created by Sponsor or PMO
High-level document
Required before planning begins

details.definition: A document issued by the project initiator or sponsor that formally authorizes the project and provides the Project Manager with authority to apply organizational resources.

who creates it.creator: Project Sponsor or PMO
who creates it.PM role: The Project Manager may assist but cannot approve the charter

important notes: The charter is created before detailed planning
Without a charter, the project should not proceed
details.real world example: Similar to an official approval letter from executive leadership that authorizes a manager to start and lead a strategic initiative.

exam_tips: The Project Charter authorizes the project and grants authority to the Project Manager. It is created by the Sponsor, not the Project Manager.

title: Scope Management
summary: Scope Management ensures that the project includes all the work required—and only the work required—to complete the project successfully.
key concepts: Product Scope defines features and functions
Project Scope defines the work required
Scope Baseline = Scope Statement + WBS + WBS Dictionary
Gold Plating = adding features beyond requirements

wbs.definition: A hierarchical decomposition of the total project scope into manageable components.
rules: Lowest level is the Work Package
All work must be included in the WBS

scope issues.scope creep: Unauthorized changes to scope without formal approval
scope issues.gold plating: Adding extra features not requested by the customer

validate vs control.control scope: Monitoring and managing changes to scope baseline

exam tips: WBS is deliverable-based, not activity-based. Validate Scope = customer acceptance. Control Scope = prevent scope creep.

title: Schedule Management
summary: Schedule Management involves defining, sequencing, estimating, and controlling project activities to ensure timely completion.
key_concepts: Activities are derived from Work Packages
Dependencies define task order
Critical Path determines project duration
Float represents scheduling flexibility
Schedule Baseline is used for performance measurement

critical path.definition: The longest path through the project network that determines the shortest project duration.
rules: Activities on the critical path have zero float
Delays on critical path delay the project
There can be more than one critical path

schedule compression.crashing: Adding resources to shorten duration (increases cost)

exam tips: Critical Path = longest path with zero float. Crashing increases cost. Fast Tracking increases risk.

title: Estimating Techniques
summary: Estimating techniques are used to predict project duration, cost, and resource requirements with varying levels of accuracy.
key concepts: Different techniques provide different accuracy levels

analogous.definition: Uses historical data from similar projects

three_point.definition: Uses optimistic, most likely, and pessimistic estimates

bottom_up.definition: Estimates at the lowest level and aggregates upward

exam tips: PERT formula = (O + 4M + P) / 6. Bottom-Up is most accurate but time-consuming. Analogous is fastest but least accurate.

title: Cost Management and Earned Value Management (EVM)
summary: Cost Management includes estimating, budgeting, and controlling project costs. Earned Value Management (EVM) integrates scope, schedule, and cost to measure project performance.
key concepts: Cost and schedule performance can be measured quantitatively

interpretation.positive variance: Good (under budget or ahead of schedule)

forecasting.EAC: Estimate at Completion = BAC / CPI (most common)

insight: EVM integrates scope, schedule, and cost

exam_tips: CV = EV - AC, SV = EV - PV. CPI/SPI >1 is good. EAC = BAC / CPI is most common formula.

title: Quality Management
summary: Quality Management ensures that project deliverables meet requirements. It includes Quality Assurance (process-focused) and Quality Control (product-focused).
key concepts: Quality = fitness for use and conformance to requirements
Cost of Quality includes prevention, appraisal, and failure
Quality must be planned, not inspected

QA vs QC.QC: Detects defects through inspection and testing

exam_tips: QA = prevent defects. QC = detect defects. QC produces Verified Deliverables; Validate Scope produces Accepted Deliverables.

title: Risk Management
summary: Risk Management is the process of identifying, analyzing, and responding to uncertainties that could affect project objectives.
key concepts: Issue = risk that has already occurred
exam_tips: Risk = uncertain event. Threat responses: Avoid > Transfer > Mitigate > Accept. Contingency = known risks; Management reserve = unknown risks.

title: Integrated Change Control
summary: Integrated Change Control is the process of reviewing, approving, or rejecting changes to the project. It ensures that all changes are managed in a structured and controlled manner.
key_concepts: No change is implemented without formal approval
Change Control Board (CCB) reviews major changes
Baselines are updated only after approval
All approved changes must be documented
Prevents scope creep

important rules: Never implement changes based on verbal approval
All affected documents must be updated
Changes may impact scope, schedule, cost, and quality

ccb.definition: A group responsible for reviewing and approving changes

exam_tips: Never implement changes without approval. Even if a sponsor verbally agrees, formal change approval is required.

title: Procurement Management
summary: Procurement Management involves acquiring goods and services from external vendors. Choosing the right contract type is critical to managing risk.
key concepts: Clearly defined scope improves procurement success
Formal closure of contracts is required

fixed price.description: Price is fixed; seller bears most risk

cost reimbursable.description: Buyer pays costs; buyer bears most risk

time material.description: Hybrid model; payment based on time and materials
time material.risk: Shared, but often leans toward buyer risk

exam_tips: Fixed Price = seller risk. Cost Plus = buyer risk. T&M = hybrid. Always formally close contracts.

title: Communications Management
summary: Communications Management ensures that project information is created, distributed, and understood effectively among stakeholders.
key_concepts: Project Managers spend most of their time communicating
Effective communication is critical for project success
Different stakeholders require different communication approaches
Communication must be planned and structured

communication types.push: Information is sent to recipients (e.g., emails, reports)
communication types.pull: Information is accessed by stakeholders when needed

exam_tips: Channels = n(n-1)/2. Push = send, Pull = retrieve, Interactive = two-way. Communication must be tailored to stakeholders.

title: Project Closure
summary: Project Closure is the final phase where all project work is completed, deliverables are formally accepted, and the project is officially closed.
key_concepts: Closure is a formal process, not automatic
Customer or sponsor acceptance is required
Lessons learned must be documented
Resources must be released
Project documents must be archived

closure types.successful completion: Project objectives achieved and deliverables accepted
closure types.early termination: Project stopped before completion due to business or strategic reasons

important rules: Closure must happen even if the project is terminated early
Lessons learned should be captured before team disbanding
details.phase gate: Project phases may include formal closure and review before proceeding

exam_tips: Closure sequence: Acceptance → Lessons Learned → Release Resources → Archive. Always close formally, even if terminated.

title: Organizational Process Assets (OPA) and Enterprise Environmental Factors (EEF)
summary: OPAs and EEFs are key inputs in project management. OPAs are internal assets that can be used and updated, while EEFs are environmental factors that influence the project and cannot be controlled.
key_concepts: OPAs are internal and reusable
EEFs can be internal or external but are not controllable
OPAs support execution
EEFs influence or constrain decisions

opa.definition: Processes, policies, templates, and knowledge bases within the organization

eef.definition: Conditions that influence the project but are outside the control of the project team
characteristics: Can have positive or negative impact

exam_tips: If it is a template or document → OPA. If it is a condition you cannot control → EEF.

title: Stakeholder Management
summary: Stakeholder Management involves identifying, analyzing, and engaging stakeholders to ensure their needs and expectations are addressed throughout the project.
key_concepts: Stakeholders influence project success
Must be identified early and continuously
Different stakeholders require different engagement strategies
Engagement levels must be managed actively

details.goal: Move stakeholders toward supportive or leading

exam_tips: High Power + High Interest = Manage closely. Stakeholders must be identified continuously, not only at the start.

title: Leadership in Project Management
summary: Leadership in project management is the ability to guide, influence, and motivate the team and stakeholders to achieve project objectives beyond formal authority.
key_concepts: Leadership is different from management
Influence is more important than authority
Leadership is situational
Focus on people, not just process
Trust and communication are critical

definition.description: Leadership is the ability to influence individuals and teams to achieve a common goal while fostering motivation, trust, and collaboration.

leadership_vs_management.description: Leadership focuses on influencing people, while management focuses on controlling processes.
characteristics: PM must balance both leadership and management
Leadership is critical in uncertain environments

leadership_styles.description: Different leadership styles are used depending on team maturity and project context.
characteristics: Servant Leadership – supports and empowers the team
Transformational Leadership – inspires change and innovation
Transactional Leadership – based on rewards and performance

situational_leadership.description: Leadership style should be adapted based on team capability and project conditions.
characteristics: Crisis → more control and fast decision-making

power_and_influence.description: Power is the ability to influence others in the organization.
characteristics: Referent power – based on trust and respect
Coercive power – based on authority (least effective)

team_motivation.description: Motivating the team is a critical leadership responsibility.
characteristics: Align personal goals with project goals

examples: A Project Manager encourages the team during a tight deadline instead of pressuring them.
A leader resolves conflict by understanding both perspectives instead of imposing authority.
A PM empowers a senior team to make decisions rather than micromanaging.
exam_tips: Leadership in PMP focuses on trust, collaboration, and influence. Avoid authoritative or aggressive approaches unless absolutely necessary. Servant leadership is the preferred mindset.
